q: Under which section of Kshitij Part-2 are "Surdas ke Pad" compiled?
e: "Surdas ke Pad" is the first chapter of the Poetry Section (Kavya Khand) in Class 10 textbook Kshitij Part-2.

q: From which famous work of Surdas are the four verses in the textbook taken?
e: All four verses are taken from the "Bhramargeet" episode of Surdas’s famous work "Sursagar".

q: In which language are Surdas’s Pad composed?
e: Surdas was a poet of the Krishna Bhakti stream and composed his verses in melodious Braj Bhasha.

q: Through whom did Shri Krishna send the message of Yoga from Mathura to the Gopis?
e: After going to Mathura, instead of returning himself, Shri Krishna sent the message of Yoga to the Gopis through his friend Uddhav.

q: Whom did the Gopis mockingly call "Ati Badbhagi" (very fortunate)?
e: In the first verse, the Gopis satirically address Uddhav saying, "Uddhav, you are exceedingly fortunate."

q: What is the literal meaning of the word "Badbhagi"?
e: The literal meaning of "Badbhagi" is "fortunate", though the Gopis use it sarcastically.

q: What is meant by "Puraini Paat"?
e: In Braj Bhasha, "Puraini Paat" means "lotus leaf", which remains dry despite staying in water.

q: Describing themselves as "weak and innocent", to what did the Gopis compare themselves?
e: The Gopis say they are stuck to Krishna’s love just like ants clinging to jaggery ("Gur Chanti Jyon Pagi").

q: Whose river of love is indicated by the term "Preeti-Nadi"?
e: "Preeti-Nadi" refers to the river of Shri Krishna’s love, in which Uddhav never dipped his foot despite staying near him.

q: According to the Gopis, what happens when an oil-smeared pot is dipped in water?
o: Not even a single drop of water sticks to it
The pot becomes heavy and sinks
e: Just as not a drop of water sticks to an oil-coated pot, Uddhav remained untouched by love despite living with Krishna.

q: According to the second verse, where did the feelings of the Gopis’ hearts remain?
e: The Gopis say "Man ki man hi manjh rahi", meaning their longing to speak to Krishna remained trapped within their hearts.

q: On what basis were the Gopis enduring the agony of body and mind?
o: Out of fear of King Kansa
On the hope and promised time of Krishna’s return
On the advice of Gokul villagers
e: The Gopis endured suffering based on the expectation and time period ("Avadhi") of Krishna’s promised return.

q: In the line "Birahini birah dahi", whom does the word "Birahini" refer to?
e: Suffering from separation from Krishna, the Gopis call themselves "Birahini" (separated lovers), whose agony grew upon hearing Yoga.

q: Whom have the Gopis called "Haril ki Lakari" (the wood of the Haril bird)?
e: In the third verse, the Gopis declare Shri Krishna ("Hari") to be their sole support, just like the twig held by the Haril bird.

q: What is the special characteristic of the Haril bird?
o: It builds its nest in water
It always holds a piece of wood firmly in its claws
e: The Haril bird always grips a twig or piece of wood in its claws and never lets go, symbolizing unwavering attachment.

q: How does Uddhav’s message of Yoga feel to the Gopis upon hearing it?
e: The Gopis say listening to Yoga feels just like tasting a bitter cucumber ("Karui Kakari").

q: What did the Gopis call Yoga, saying they had neither seen, heard, nor experienced it before?
e: The Gopis refer to Yoga as a "Vyadhi" (disease/ailment) that Uddhav brought to them.

q: According to the Gopis, to whom should the teaching of Yoga be handed over?
o: To those whose minds are restless like a spinning wheel
e: The Gopis tell Uddhav to give Yoga to those whose minds spin restlessly like a wheel ("Man Chakari").

q: In the fourth verse, what do the Gopis say Shri Krishna has studied after going to Mathura?
e: The Gopis sarcastically remark that Hari (Krishna) has studied politics ("Rajneeti") in Mathura.

q: Who is referred to by the word "Madhukar" in the verse?
e: In the Bhramargeet episode, the Gopis address Uddhav indirectly using the word "Madhukar" (bumblebee).

q: According to the Gopis, what should be the true "Raj Dharam" (duty of a king)?
o: More tax should be collected from subjects
The subjects must not be tormented
e: The final line states that the true duty of a king is to ensure that the subjects are not harassed or tormented.

q: What is the meaning of the word "Aparas"?
e: "Aparas" means untouched or unaffected; Uddhav remained completely untouched by the thread of love.

q: What does the word "Taga" mean?
e: In "Saneh Taga", "Taga" means "thread", symbolizing the bond of love.

q: According to the Gopis, what did Shri Krishna steal while leaving for Mathura?
e: The Gopis say they want back their minds/hearts ("Man") which Krishna had stolen while departing.

q: In "Surdas ke Pad", whose name do the Gopis keep chanting day and night, awake or asleep?
e: The Gopis say whether awake, asleep, or dreaming, day and night they chant "Kanha-Kanha".

q: What do the Gopis mean by "Marjada na lahi"?
o: Shri Krishna did not uphold the decorum of love
e: The decorum of love demands love in return for love, which Krishna broke by sending a message of Yoga instead.

q: Whom did the Gopis refer to as "good people of earlier times" who rushed around for others’ welfare?
o: Benevolent people of olden times (satire on Uddhav)
e: The Gopis sarcastically contrast benevolent people of olden times with Uddhav, who came bearing painful Yoga.

q: In the "Bhramargeet" episode, whom does the bumblebee (Bhramar) symbolize?
e: The Gopis address Uddhav indirectly under the pretext of a bumblebee, making the bee a symbol for Uddhav.

q: Which emotion do the Gopis express towards Uddhav in the first verse?
e: In the first verse, the Gopis express sharp yet witty satire and reproach at Uddhav’s lack of love.

q: Who is known as the foremost poet of "Ashtachhap"?
e: Surdas holds the foremost position among the eight "Ashtachhap" Bhakti poets.

q: What is the meaning of the word "Paragi" in "Drishti na roop paragi"?
e: Here "Paragi" means "enchanted or captivated"—Uddhav’s eyes were never captivated by Krishna’s beauty.

q: In "Chahati hutin guhari jitahin tain, ut tain dhar bahi", what do the Gopis mean by "Dhar"?
o: The strong stream of Yoga’s message
e: From the very place (Krishna) where the Gopis hoped for rescue, the overwhelming stream of Yoga’s message flowed.

q: Which figure of speech (Alankar) is used in "Gur chanti jyon pagi"?
e: Using the comparative word "Jyon", the Gopis’ devotion is compared to ants stuck in jaggery, making it Upama Alankar.

q: Which figure of speech is used in "Preeti-Nadi"?
e: Because love is directly identified with a river without any comparative word, "Preeti-Nadi" has Rupak Alankar (Metaphor).

q: Due to the repetition of the consonant "H" in "Hamarein Hari Haril ki Lakari", which Alankar is present?
e: The repetition of the initial consonant sound "H" in "Hamarein Hari Haril" produces Anupras Alankar (Alliteration).

q: In "Ik ati chatur hute pahilain hin, ab guru granth padhae", what do the Gopis imply by "Guru Granth"?
o: Heavy treatises of politics and statecraft
e: The Gopis imply that Krishna was already clever, and now he has mastered weighty treatises of politics.

q: What is the meaning of the word "Pathae" in "Badi buddhi jani jo unki, jog-sandes pathae"?
e: In Braj Bhasha, "Pathae" means "sent"—Krishna sent the message of Yoga.

q: What is the meaning of "Jak ri" in "Kanha-Kanha jak ri"?
e: "Jak ri" (Jakari) means continuously chanting or repeating a name obsessively.

q: Which Rasa (aesthetic emotion) predominates in these verses of Surdas?
e: Due to the depiction of the Gopis’ pangs of separation from Krishna, Viyog Shringara Rasa predominates.

q: In "Man ki man hi manjh rahi", to whom are the Gopis unable to express their heart’s feelings?
o: Uddhav or anyone else (as only Krishna deserves to hear it)
e: The Gopis ask Uddhav whom else they can go and tell their innermost feelings, as they cannot be spoken to just anyone.

q: What is the Tatsama (Sanskrit) form of the word "Bitha" in "Tan man bitha sahi"?
e: "Bitha" is the Braj form of the Sanskrit/Tatsama word "Vyatha", meaning agony or suffering.

q: Why did the Gopis give the examples of "lotus leaf" and "oil pot" for Uddhav?
o: To describe the nature of Braj
To show that despite being near Krishna, he remained untouched by love
e: Just as a lotus leaf and oil pot remain dry in water, Uddhav stayed untouched by love despite living beside Krishna.

q: What is the correct meaning of the word "Dahi" in "Birahini birah dahi"?
e: Here "Dahi" (from dagdha) means "burned" or "scorched" in the fire of separation.

q: Who is called "Nand-Nandan" in "Man kram bachan Nand-Nandan ur, yah dridh kari pakari"?
e: "Nand-Nandan" means the son of Nanda, i.e., Shri Krishna, whom the Gopis hold firmly in their hearts.

q: In "Te kyon aneeti karain aapun, je aur aneeti chhudae", whom does "je aur aneeti chhudae" refer to?
e: Shri Krishna freed others from injustice (like Kansa’s tyranny), so why is he himself acting unjustly toward the Gopis?

q: In the fourth verse, what do the Gopis speak of getting back from Krishna?
e: The Gopis say they will get back their hearts/minds that Krishna stole while leaving.

q: What is the style of Surdas’s Pad?
e: All of Surdas’s verses are composed in the musical lyrical "Geya Pad" style set to classical ragas.

q: Which special quality of the Gopis is expressed in "Bhramargeet"?
e: With remarkable wit, logic, and sarcasm, the Gopis left the learned Uddhav speechless.

q: In what manner do the Gopis reject the "Jog-Sandes" (message of Yoga)?
o: Calling it unappealing, bitter, and an ailment
Accepting it as an easy path
e: Being devotees of Saguna Bhakti, the Gopis reject Nirguna Yoga by calling it a bitter cucumber and a disease.

q: In "Dheer dharahin kyon", why are the Gopis unable to keep patience?
o: Because Shri Krishna did not uphold the decorum of love
e: When Krishna himself abandoned the decorum of love by sending a Yoga message, the Gopis lost their patience.

q: When and where is Surdas believed to have been born (major view as per NCERT)?
e: According to NCERT, Surdas is believed to have been born in 1478 CE at Runkata near Mathura (another view says Sihi).

q: Who was the guru (spiritual teacher) of Surdas?
e: Surdas was a disciple of Mahaprabhu Vallabhacharya, under whose guidance he sang of Krishna’s Leelas.

q: In "Samujhi baat kahat madhukar ke, samachar sab pae", whose words gave the Gopis all the news?
e: One Gopi tells another that from the very words of this bee (Uddhav), they understood everything and got all news of Krishna.

q: What does "Dolat dhae" mean in "Par hit dolat dhae"?
o: Used to run about / rush around
e: "Dolat dhae" means rushing or running about eagerly for the welfare of others.

q: Which Alankar is present in "Suni-Suni"?
e: The repetition of the exact same word "Suni" in the same meaning creates Punrukti Prakash Alankar.

q: To which stream of Bhakti poetry does Surdas principally belong?
e: Surdas is the crowning poet of the Saguna Krishna-Bhakti stream of the Bhakti period in Hindi literature.

q: For whom is the word "Tinahin" used in the line "Tinahin lai saumpau"?
o: Those whose minds are fickle like a spinning wheel
e: The Gopis say their own minds are steady in Krishna, so Yoga should be given to those ("Tinahin") with fickle minds.

q: What does the word "Pagi" mean in "Gur chanti jyon pagi"?
e: "Pagi" means stuck, immersed, or absorbed—just like an ant absorbed in jaggery.

q: Which spiritual path did Uddhav advocate, which the Gopis rejected?
o: Path of Nirguna Brahma and Yoga
e: Uddhav advocated Nirguna (formless) Brahma and Yoga, whereas the Gopis were devoted to Saguna love for Krishna.

q: What kind of love of the Gopis is depicted in "Surdas ke Pad"?
e: The Gopis’ love for Krishna is completely single-minded, exclusive, and selfless, unshaken by Yoga.

q: Excerpt: "Just as a lotus leaf stays in water without getting stained, and an oil pot gets no water drop on it." — Whom are both these analogies used to satirize?
o: Shri Krishna for forgetting the Gopis in Mathura
Nand Baba for not stopping Uddhav
Uddhav, who stayed near Krishna (ocean of love) yet remained untouched by love
e: Both illustrations satirize Uddhav’s emotional detachment despite living right beside Krishna, the embodiment of love.

q: Context: The Gopis tell Uddhav that "not tormenting one’s subjects is the true duty of a king." What do the Gopis want to remind Shri Krishna through this statement?
o: That he should make Balarama the king
That he should build a new palace in Gokul
That as king of Mathura, he must not torment the Gopis with separation and Yoga messages
e: Since Krishna is now the ruler of Mathura and the Gopis are his subjects, he must not inflict further pain on them.

q: Excerpt: "From the very direction we wanted to call for rescue, the flood flowed." — If a person expects help from a trusted friend in crisis and that friend worsens the problem, which idea in this line does it match?
o: Receiving timely help from a friend
The very protector becoming the source of agony
The crisis ending on its own
Getting help from a third person
e: The Gopis expected Krishna to save them from separation, yet his own Yoga message became the cause of greater pain.

q: Context: In the third verse, the Gopis say, "Hand this over to those whose minds are like a spinning wheel." What mental state of their own did they clarify through this suggestion?
o: That their minds are completely steady and focused on Krishna, so they need no Yoga
That their minds are very fickle
That they are ready to learn Yoga
That they are eager to visit Mathura
e: Yoga aims to steady a restless mind; since the Gopis’ minds are already fixed on Krishna, Yoga is unnecessary for them.

q: Excerpt: "Uddhav, you are exceedingly fortunate." — If a student tells a failing friend, "Wow, you turned out to be a great scholar!", which linguistic device matches this line of Surdas?
e: Superficially it sounds like praise ("fortunate"), but the real intent is ironic mockery of Uddhav’s loveless state.

q: Context: "Like ants stuck to jaggery" — What helplessness and devotion do the Gopis prove using this example?
o: Just as jaggery dissolves in water
Just as an ant can fly
Just as an ant cannot separate from jaggery, the Gopis cannot detach from Krishna’s love even if they try
Just as an ant hides in winter
e: An ant remains clinging to jaggery even at the cost of its life; similarly, the Gopis’ love for Krishna is inseparable.

q: Excerpt: "Now hearing these Yoga messages repeatedly, the separated lovers burn in separation." — What role did the Yoga message play for the Gopis here?
o: Of pouring ghee into the fire of separation
e: The Gopis were enduring separation hoping for Krishna’s return, but the Yoga message added fuel to their fire of separation.

q: Context: "Listening to the bee’s words, we got all the news" — Why does one Gopi say this to another at the start of the fourth verse?
o: Because Uddhav’s words clearly revealed Krishna’s changed mindset and political diplomacy
Because Uddhav read out a royal scroll
Because another messenger ran in from Mathura
Because Krishna himself was standing at the door
e: As soon as Uddhav spoke of Yoga, the Gopis realized Krishna had become a calculating politician rather than a simple lover.

q: Context: If someone breaks an implicit promise of mutual affection, in the Gopis’ words, what is that person violating?
e: The Gopis termed Krishna’s betrayal of love’s expectation as breaking "Marjada" (decorum).

q: Excerpt: "For us, Hari is the twig of the Haril bird..." — What kind of relationship between devotee and God emerges from this statement?
o: A relation of fear and doubt
The devotee accepting God in thought, deed, and word as the sole anchor of life
A relation based on profit and loss
e: Holding onto Krishna through thought, deed, and speech reflects unwavering, total devotion.

q: Context: The Gopis say, "Now we will get back our minds which he stole while leaving." What underlying feeling is hidden here?
o: Indignant reproach—if Krishna has abandoned love, he should return the hearts he took
e: It is a dignified reproach: since Krishna now practices politics, he ought to return the hearts he stole.

q: Excerpt: "Listening to Yoga feels like a bitter cucumber." — On which sense is the sensory imagery built here?
o: Combining hearing with taste imagery to convey extreme distaste
e: Just as bitter cucumber is spit out immediately on tasting, Yoga is rejected the moment it reaches their ears.

q: Context: If Uddhav had succeeded in teaching Nirguna Yoga over Saguna love, what would happen to the central theme of Surdas’s Bhramargeet?
o: Then Surdas would become a heroic poet
Then Gopis would become queens of Mathura
Then the triumph of Bhakti (devotion) over dry Gyan (knowledge), the core theme, would not be established
e: The central purpose of Bhramargeet is to establish the superiority of Saguna devotion and love over dry Nirguna Yoga.

q: Excerpt: "The expected time of return was the basis on which we endured bodily and mental agony." — If a loved one gives a return date to a waiting family, what role does that date serve?
o: An anchor/support to live and endure hardship
e: The expected time ("Avadhi") acted as the emotional anchor helping the Gopis bear their suffering.

q: Context: By asking why he who freed others from injustice is now doing injustice himself, what episode do the Gopis point to?
o: Shri Krishna liberating Mathura from tyrants like Kansa
e: Krishna ended Kansa’s tyranny in Mathura to uphold justice, which is why the Gopis question his present unfairness.

q: Excerpt: "To whom should we go and speak, O Uddhav; it cannot be uttered." — Which psychological truth does this reflect?
o: Deep personal love and pain cannot be laid bare before just anyone
e: Intimate feelings of the heart can only be shared with someone empathetic, not with an unfeeling philosopher.

q: Context: "The subjects should not be oppressed" — What relevant message does this line carry for modern democratic governance?
o: Military might is the only basis of a state
Rulers should stay away from citizens
A ruler’s foremost duty is public welfare and protecting citizens from oppression
e: This timeless maxim emphasizes that the purpose of authority is protecting and serving people, not oppressing them.

q: Excerpt: "You brought us an ailment we never saw, heard, or experienced." — If medicine is forced upon someone who does not need it, what does it become in the Gopis’ eyes?
e: The Gopis had no need for Yoga since they were already absorbed in love; hence unwanted Yoga felt like an ailment.

q: Context: "Neither is your mind loving" and "nor is your gaze enchanted by beauty" — What aspect of Uddhav’s personality do these phrases reveal?
e: Uddhav lives purely on dry intellect; neither affection nor aesthetic sensitivity has awakened in his heart.

q: Excerpt: "Great indeed is his wisdom, as seen in his sending the Yoga message." — What are the Gopis mocking about Krishna here?
o: Krishna’s "great wisdom" in sending dry Yoga to love-lorn women
e: They sarcastically mock Krishna’s "superior intellect" for prescribing dry Yoga to women pining in love.

q: Context: Across the four verses, the Gopis’ tone shifts. What change appears in their tone by the fourth verse?
o: They fall at Uddhav’s feet and accept Yoga
Moving beyond complaint and longing, they raise sharp logical questions about Krishna’s politics and royal duty
e: Moving from satire, longing, and steadfast devotion, by the fourth verse they corner Uddhav with ethical questions of Rajdharma.

q: Excerpt: "Awake, asleep, in dreams, day and night, chanting Kanha-Kanha." — Which psychological state does this resemble?
o: Complete absorption of both conscious and subconscious mind in one beloved
e: Remembering Krishna both while awake (conscious) and in dreams (subconscious) shows total emotional immersion.

q: Context: Which event in the text justifies the title "Bhramargeet"?
o: Breaking of a beehive in Gokul
The arrival of a bumblebee during the dialogue, which the Gopis address to deliver their satire at Uddhav
Uddhav writing a song on a bee
e: While Uddhav was preaching, a bumblebee flew in, giving the Gopis a symbolic target ("Madhukar") to aim their wit at Uddhav.

q: Excerpt: "You did not dip your foot in the river of love." — What expectation did the Gopis have from Uddhav that went unfulfilled?
o: That having lived with Krishna, he would understand the value of love and empathize with the Gopis
That he would bathe in the Yamuna
That he would row a boat in Gokul
e: The Gopis expected Krishna’s close friend to grasp the essence of love, yet he proved utterly ignorant of it.

q: Context: In "Man ki man hi manjh rahi", which suppressed desire remained unfulfilled due to Krishna not returning?
o: Desire to sit on Mathura’s throne
Desire to debate scriptures with Uddhav
The desire to meet Krishna and share the joys and sorrows of their love and separation
e: The Gopis had waited to pour out their hearts when Krishna returned, but Uddhav’s arrival left that wish unfulfilled.

q: Excerpt: "Good were the people of yore, who ran about for others’ welfare." — If a royal envoy imposes a new burden instead of relief, how does he fit this satire?
o: Opposite of altruistic ancestors—one who adds to others’ distress
e: Unlike benevolent people of earlier times, Uddhav traveled far only to distress the Gopis with Yoga.

q: Context: Which poetic device/skill is most evident in the use of the word "Madhukar" in Surdas’s verses?
o: Anyokti / symbolism — addressing Uddhav indirectly under the pretext of the bee
e: Using the bumblebee ("Madhukar") as a pretext to criticize Uddhav exemplifies Anyokti (indirect address) and symbolism.

q: Excerpt: "Surdas says, we are helpless and simple women." — Why do the Gopis call themselves weak and simple despite defeating Uddhav in debate?
o: With humility and irony, to show they are helpless in love yet free from the pride of dry intellect
Because they truly could not speak
Because they did not know Braj Bhasha
e: By calling themselves simple, they gently deflate Uddhav’s intellectual pride while elevating sincere devotion.

q: Context: After studying all four verses, if Uddhav’s final scene were staged in a play, what would his expression be?
o: Humbled, amazed, and speechless before the Gopis’ devotion and wit
e: Before the Gopis’ steadfast love, wit, and ethical reasoning, the proud Uddhav stands humbled and speechless.

q: Excerpt: Expressions like "it tain... ut tain..." and "man ki man hi..." bring which quality to Surdas’s poetic language?
o: Emotional flow, musicality, and natural conversational charm
e: Such idiomatic Braj Bhasha expressions lend lyrical flow, musicality, and lively conversational realism.

q:
Assertion (A): By calling Uddhav "Ati Badbhagi", the Gopis genuinely praised him.
Reason (R): Uddhav remained untouched by the bond of love despite living in the company of Shri Krishna.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Assertion (A) is false because the Gopis used "Badbhagi" sarcastically, not as genuine praise. Reason (R) is true.

q:
Assertion (A): The Gopis compared Uddhav’s Yoga message to a bitter cucumber.
Reason (R): The Gopis were immersed in exclusive devotion to Saguna Shri Krishna and found Nirguna Yoga distasteful.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) correctly explains why the Yoga message felt like a bitter cucumber to them.

q:
Assertion (A): The Gopis described themselves as ants stuck to jaggery.
Reason (R): They are so deeply absorbed in Krishna’s love that they cannot separate from him while alive.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) accurately explains the unbreakable devotion symbolized by ants and jaggery.

q:
Assertion (A): The Gopis tell Uddhav to hand over the teaching of Yoga to those whose minds are like a spinning wheel.
Reason (R): The Gopis’ own minds were completely steady and focused on Shri Krishna.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both are true; since the Gopis’ minds were steadfast in Krishna, they deemed Yoga suitable only for restless minds.

q:
Assertion (A): According to the second verse, the Gopis’ feelings remained confined to their hearts.
Reason (R): The Gopis wanted to express their love to Shri Krishna, but instead of coming himself, he sent Uddhav.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both are true, and (R) explains why the Gopis’ innermost feelings stayed unspoken inside their hearts.

q:
Assertion (A): According to the Gopis, they can no longer hold patience.
Reason (R): Shri Krishna did not uphold the decorum of love after going to Mathura and sent a message of Yoga.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both are true and connected: because Krishna broke the decorum of love, the Gopis lost their patience.

q:
Assertion (A): Coming from Mathura, Uddhav preached Saguna Bhakti to the Gopis.
Reason (R): Shri Krishna wanted the Gopis to overcome the pain of separation and adopt the path of knowledge.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Assertion (A) is false because Uddhav preached Nirguna Yoga, not Saguna Bhakti. Reason (R) is true.

q:
Assertion (A): The language of Surdas’s Pad is melodious Braj Bhasha.
Reason (R): Bhakti poetry and folk songs related to Krishna’s Leelas in the Braj region were traditionally composed in Braj Bhasha.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both are true, and the poetic tradition of the Braj region explains why Surdas composed his verses in Braj Bhasha.

q:

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

e: Assertion (A) is false because it refers to water in a vessel/pond, not raindrops. Reason (R) is true.

q: In the first verse, which three analogies/metaphors does Surdas use via the Gopis to create a sharp contrast around Uddhav?
o: Haril’s twig, bitter cucumber, and spinning wheel
Lotus leaf, oil pot, and river of love (for Uddhav), contrasted with jaggery-ant (for Gopis)
Politics, heavy texts, and royal duty
e: The three images of detachment (lotus leaf, oil pot, dry foot by the love-river) stand in stark contrast to the Gopis’ image of ants stuck in jaggery.

q: Which line best exemplifies "Vakrokti" (oblique/ironic expression) in Surdas’s Bhramargeet verses?
o: "In thought, deed, and word, Nanda’s son in our hearts"
"Awake, asleep, in dream, day and night"
"True royal duty is that subjects are not tormented"
e: Calling Uddhav "exceedingly fortunate" while actually implying he is most unfortunate is the finest instance of Vakrokti.

q: Considering the sequential structure of the four verses as a dramatic argument, what is the correct progression?
o: (1) Bitter cucumber → (2) Lotus leaf → (3) Plea → (4) Guru Granth
(1) Acceptance of Yoga → (2) Departure to Mathura → (3) Slaying Kansa → (4) Coronation
(1) Satire on Uddhav’s lovelessness → (2) Longing and broken decorum → (3) Unwavering devotion & rejection of Yoga → (4) Final critique of Krishna’s politics & Rajdharma
e: Surdas masterfully structures the four verses from initial satire to emotional agony, steadfast faith, and finally ethical critique.

q: From "Hari has studied politics" to "the subjects must not be tormented", from a lover’s role, to which role do the Gopis shift their evaluation of Krishna?
o: To that of an ordinary cowherd
To that of a responsible ruler/king bound by Rajdharma
e: They evaluate Krishna as the king of Mathura rather than merely a lover, holding him accountable to Rajdharma.

q: What psychological effect does the repeated use of reduplicated words like "suni-suni" and "Kanha-Kanha" create in Surdas’s poetry?
o: Intensity of emotion, continuity, and deep sense of mental restlessness
e: Reduplication conveys relentless repetition—the Yoga sermon ringing endlessly and Krishna’s name echoing incessantly.

q: In selecting symbols like thread ("taga"), dipping ("boryau"), ailment ("vyadhi"), twig ("lakari"), and bitter cucumber, which trait of Surdas’s poetry emerges?
o: Use of vivid imagery drawn directly from everyday rural life and folk experience
e: Lotus leaf, oil pot, jaggery-ants, Haril bird, cucumber, and spinning wheel are vivid, earthy images from rural folk life.

q: Behind "Gur chanti jyon pagi" in the first verse lies a subtle tragedy. What is that subtle tragedy?
o: The ant grows big eating jaggery
The ant clings to jaggery’s sweetness until death; likewise, the Gopis’ love reaches total self-sacrifice
e: An ant stuck in jaggery cannot free itself and perishes in it, subtly hinting at the life-consuming depth of the Gopis’ devotion.

q: Comparative question: What is the key difference between Lakshman’s satire in Tulsidas’s dialogue and the Gopis’ satire in Surdas’s Pad?
o: Lakshman uses Braj and Gopis use Awadhi
Lakshman’s satire is infused with heroic pride and provocation, while the Gopis’ satire is steeped in separation-agony, love, and tenderness
e: Lakshman’s wit belongs to a heroic confrontation, whereas the Gopis’ irony rises from tender separation and Bhakti.

q: By saying "whose minds are like a spinning wheel", how do the Gopis expose the limitation/scope of Nirguna Yoga?
o: They declare Yoga mandatory for all
They establish that Yoga is merely a tool to steady a wandering mind, whereas Bhakti is already pure, steady attainment
They say spinning minds can never be happy
They call Yoga mere physical exercise
e: Philosophically, they frame Yoga as a remedial tool for restless minds and Bhakti as the higher, already-attained stillness.

q: Why has Surdas placed his signature name ("Sur" or "Surdas") at the end of each of the four verses?
o: It was the medieval Bhakti poetic convention (Bhanit/Chhap) to mark authorship and personal devotion
e: Medieval Bhakti poets traditionally wove their poetic signature ("Chhap") into the closing line to signify authorship and devotion.

q: In the fourth verse, how do the Gopis bring the dramatic quality of "Sakhi-Samvad" (dialogue among friends) while addressing Uddhav?
o: By writing a letter to Krishna
By speaking to one another about Krishna’s politics while indirectly targeting Uddhav
e: In the fourth verse, the Gopis converse among themselves ("Sakhi-Samvad"), sidelining Uddhav while sharpening their satire.

q: What two layers of meaning in "Marjada" ("Marjada na lahi") enrich the poetic beauty of the second verse?
o: (1) Krishna failing to uphold the reciprocity of love, and (2) the Gopis’ patience/social restraint giving way
e: Both Krishna’s breach of love’s reciprocity and the resulting collapse of the Gopis’ restraint deepen the line’s meaning.

q: If Uddhav’s character is viewed as a journey from pride to humility, what was his pride centered on in these verses?
o: Pride in his Nirguna knowledge, Yoga discipline, and being Krishna’s wisest confidant
e: In the broader narrative, Krishna sent Uddhav to Gokul specifically to humble his intellectual pride and teach him the essence of love.

q: What structural quality is shared by the opening lines "Hamarein Hari Haril ki Lakari" and "Man ki man hi manjh rahi"?
o: Both act like a refrain (Tek) encapsulating the entire emotional core of the verse in a single line
e: In lyrical Pad tradition, the opening line serves as the "Tek" (refrain) summarizing the verse’s central theme.

q: In "Why should he act unjustly who freed others from injustice?", which principle of justice do the Gopis invoke?
o: The king is above the law
Moral consistency: the champion of justice cannot himself become a perpetrator of injustice
e: The Gopis hold Krishna to the very moral standard he set by ending tyranny, demanding ethical consistency.

q: Which phonological feature of Braj Bhasha enhances the rhythm and sweetness in Surdas’s Pad?
o: Heavy clustering of harsh retroflex sounds
Abundance of soft consonants, smooth liquids, and nasalizations (like manjh, jyon, hau)
e: Braj Bhasha’s soft syllables, gentle liquids, and nasalized vowels create exceptional musical sweetness.

q: In "Birahini birah dahi" and "ut tain dhar bahi", how are opposing natural elements poetically combined?
o: Contrast of fire (burning) and stream (flowing)—ironically, the stream of Yoga inflamed rather than cooled the fire of separation
e: Normally a stream quenches fire, yet here the stream of Yoga intensified the fire of separation—a striking poetic paradox.

q: In "Aparas rahat saneh taga tain", what subtle meaning is embedded in the phrase "Saneh Taga" (thread of love)?
o: Love is a delicate yet strong invisible thread binding hearts; Uddhav remained untouched even by its brush
Love is a rope for tying cattle
Love is cloth sold in markets
Love is merely an empty word
e: "Taga" (thread) symbolizes both delicacy and binding strength; "Saneh Taga" uses metaphor to express love’s subtle bond.

q: If writing an essay on "Bhakti vs. Gyan" based on this chapter, what philosophical conclusion do Surdas’s Gopis uphold?
o: Knowledge alone is truth and love is illusion
Sincere devotion and love of the heart are far more vibrant and superior to dry intellectualism and austere Yoga
e: The entire philosophy of Bhramargeet affirms the supremacy of heartfelt devotion over dry intellectualism.

q: In the fourth verse, when the Gopis say they will take back the hearts Krishna stole—have they truly decided to forget Krishna?
o: Yes, they went to Mathura with Uddhav
No, it is "Pranay-Maan" (loving indignation); demanding their hearts back is meant to make Krishna feel his insensitivity
Yes, they will worship someone else
e: In love, affectionate indignation ("Maan") is natural when neglected; deep down, they know their hearts cannot leave Krishna.

q: Why do Surdas’s verses abound in "Drishtant" (illustration) and "Udaharan" (example) figures of speech?
o: Because the Gopis forgot Braj Bhasha
So the Gopis can refute abstract Yoga and explain love through concrete, familiar everyday examples
e: Concrete illustrations like the lotus leaf, oil pot, Haril twig, and bitter cucumber make the Gopis’ arguments irrefutable.

q: How does the thought progress across the two consecutive lines comparing Yoga to a "bitter cucumber" and then calling it a "disease/ailment"?
o: First they call Yoga merely "distasteful" (bitter cucumber), then escalate to declaring it a harmful "ailment" (Vyadhi)
e: This shows poetic escalation (climax)—moving from mere distaste (bitter cucumber) to total rejection as a disease (Vyadhi).

q: Where does the seed of "people-centric governance" appear in the Gopis’ dialogue in "Surdas ke Pad"?
o: In "Man ki man hi manjh rahi"
In "True Rajdharma is that subjects are not tormented", holding the ruler accountable for citizens’ well-being
e: This line rejects despotic rule, binding the sovereign to the moral obligation of protecting subjects from distress.

q: In the line "Avadhi adhar aas aavan ki", which Alankar is clearly present due to the repetition of the vowel "A/Aa"?
e: The successive repetition of initial "A/Aa" sounds in "Avadhi adhar aas aavan" creates Anupras Alankar.

q: In Bhramargeet, addressing Uddhav via the black bumblebee ("Madhukar") carries satire on both color and nature. What is it?
o: Both Uddhav and Krishna are dark-complexioned, and like the bee that sips nectar and flies away, they seem fickle and heartless
Because the bee comes out only at night
Because the bee lives in water
e: Surdas’s Gopis link the dark complexion of Krishna/Uddhav with the bee’s proverbial fickleness after taking nectar.

q: What role does the end-rhyme ("anuragi", "lagi", "paragi", "pagi") play in the first verse?
o: Consistent end-rhyme sustains musicality, rhythm, and thematic unity across the verse
e: The consistent "-agi" end-rhyme makes the verse highly musical, rhythmic, and memorable.

q: Based on the text, what core argument was Uddhav offering to persuade the Gopis to adopt Yoga?
o: That dance and music alone lead to God
That they should leave Braj for the Himalayas
That through meditation on formless (Nirguna) Brahma via Yoga, they could free themselves from the pain of separation
e: Uddhav’s thesis was that meditating on the formless Nirguna Brahma via Yoga would cure their pain of separation.

q: Why is the Gopis’ eloquence in "Surdas ke Pad" regarded as the pinnacle of "Upalambha Kavya" (poetry of affectionate reproach)?
o: Because without malice or bitterness, it uniquely blends loving reproach, wit, logic, and poignant pathos
e: In Upalambha Kavya, love shines through every reproach; even in sharp satire, the Gopis’ devotion never wavers.

q: Who called Surdas "Pushtimarg ka Jahaj" (the ship of Pushtimarg) in Bhakti literary history?
o: Goswami Vitthalnath (at the time of Surdas’s passing)
e: At Surdas’s passing, Vitthalnath (son of Vallabhacharya) famously declared that "the ship of Pushtimarg is departing."

q: In the context of Class 10 board exams, if asked "What is the central message of the Gopis’ reproaches to Uddhav?", what is the most accurate conclusion?
o: True love and devotion cannot be bound by dry logic, politics, or Yoga; sincerity and moral decorum are supreme in love
Politics is always greater than love
Yoga always brings joy in every situation
Life in Mathura is better than Gokul
e: The essence of all four verses is that pure devotion and love’s integrity stand far above dry knowledge, Yoga, and politics.
